name: The Jesuit method: discipline, education, and missionary zeal
plain_explanation: Loyola, a former soldier, organized the Jesuit order on military lines, with strict obedience to the General and a self-conception of waging 'warfare against heresy.' Their effectiveness came less from theology than from organization: disciplined propaganda, skillful and lenient confession practice, missionary success (especially in the Far East), and above all excellent education, which gave them a lasting hold on the minds of the young.
precise_definition: Russell's summary: the Jesuits 'were disciplined, able, completely devoted to the cause, and skilful propagandists'; 'whenever theology did not interfere, the education they gave was the best obtainable.'
why_it_mattered: This is Russell's explanation for how the Counter-Reformation checked Protestantism's early rapid success; it also sets up a direct narrative link forward, since Jesuit education is credited with teaching Descartes more mathematics than he could otherwise have learned.
historical_origin: Founded by Ignatius of Loyola; influential from the Council of Trent onward.
examples: Jesuit missionary work in the Far East
Jesuit dominance of education, later benefiting Descartes
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly foreshadows Chapter IX's account of Descartes's Jesuit education at La Flèche.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The Jesuits also urged Catholic princes toward persecution and helped re-establish the Inquisition, including in Italy.
